blogs.content: Don’t Call It a Decision Model - TypeSafe AI Blog TypeSafe AI Enterprise Thoughts Company Docs API console Contact us API console Docs Menu ∵ Back Thoughts Thoughts Don’t Call It a Decision Model Nov 3, 2026 Nov 3, 2026 Nov 3, 2026 Jev makes judgments , code makes decisions . Allie Laabs, DevRel, TypeSafe We love that people have recognized the importance of the new category of models that Jev pioneered. It’s unsurprising that the term “decision models” has caught on as a name. When you first see Jev pick an option from a list, it’s easy to see it as making decisions. And indeed, we have used the word “decision” in our own education materials! So why is TypeSafe holding firm on calling Jev a System One model instead of a decision model? Let’s talk about it. The System One name comes from the concept Daniel Kahneman popularized in his book Thinking, Fast and Slow . System 1 thinking is fast and intuitive. System 2 is slower and more deliberate. With Jev, the emphasis is on fast, focused judgments, hence the System One name. It’s about where Jev fits in a system Let’s break down what a typical system is, using the metaphor of circuits: inputs on the left (your data, application state, etc), they flow into logic, and then outputs on the right. Let’s use a simplified version of the Customer Service workflow from our evals page as an example. The naive approach to using Jev in this workflow would be to place the entire decision in to a single Jev question: When people first see Jev, this is how they imagine it fitting in to systems: give it all of your state, and have it make a decision about what should happen . This often looks like one big Choice question, and stuffing lots of semantic descriptions of business logic and caveats in to the criteria field. While this can work, you will quickly find yourself engaging in what we call prompt gymnastics : tweaking these long explanations of conditions over and over to get each edge case handled. And then the next day you get some input you hadn’t thought of, the system fails, and you’re back to stuffing more caveats and clarifications in to criteria prose. What’s happening here is trying to put intelligence at the wrong layer of abstraction. Your system already knows the criteria for each of your expected outcomes, and only some of it actually requires judgement. The rest is cold, hard logic: When Exit reports an unauthorized charge Fraud team: freeze & dispute asks for a person, or threatens legal action Hand to a person wants money back, claim eligible, ≤ $25 Refund now wants money back, claim eligible, over $25 Refunds team reviews wants to cancel, subscription active, open to an offer Offer to stay otherwise Answer & continue So where does Jev fit in to this kind of system? To understand the answer, we need to peek inside to see what a decision is actually made of: Peel off the cap Decisions in a system are rarely one atomic choice. Peel off the cap and we find wires running from the inputs through nodes of code and nodes of judgment . Decisions in software, workflows, and business are built this way. Checking “claim eligible, unpaid” is math. Answering “does the user want money back?” takes judgment. That’s where Jev belongs, and it’s exactly what we mean by System One: the quick intuitive judgments a knowledgeable person makes in seconds. Code is great for answering what it can answer exactly. Jev answers only the small questions code can’t. Logic then combines those answers into the decision. It’s the combination of both judgement and code that allows a system to make reliable, observable decisions. Why Build It This Way 1. Clarity of design Reliable systems require a clear understanding of how decisions are made. They know which positions to hold, when an exception is justified, and when changing circumstances call for a new approach. Skills capture that expertise in instructions and supporting materials that guide how the Legora Agent approaches an assignment. They bring that institutional knowledge into more of the team’s work, helping lawyers apply best practices more consistently across projects. With less time spent piecing together precedents or repeating routine steps, lawyers have more time to think through strategy, consider the questions that require their judgment, and advise their clients. The ability to extend that expertise across a firm or in-house team makes the best lawyers even more valuable. As they encounter new problems, learn from experience, and respond to changing circumstances, they can capture what they know in Skills, make it available to colleagues, and update it as their expertise evolves. Firms and in-house teams that make the most of their best lawyers’ expertise will have an advantage in serving their clients and businesses. Make your best lawyers’ expertise available to everyone Imagine an in-house lawyer at a technology company reviewing a customer agreement. Their team has captured its preferred liability positions and escalation rules in a Skill. The Agent uses that guidance to propose amendments and flag departures for review. The lawyer has an established approach to work from, shaped by colleagues who understand the business and its negotiating priorities. Rather than piecing together precedents or repeating routine steps, they can spend more time considering whether the position fits this customer and these commercial terms. A colleague can draw on that expertise without reconstructing the history of previous negotiations or asking the author to explain the same position again. The reviewing lawyer still decides how to handle the agreement, but they start with the reasoning and guidance the team has developed through experience. Your best lawyers play a critical role in evolving Skills Now suppose the same liability exception keeps appearing across customer agreements. The legal team repeatedly approves a departure from its standard position. An experienced lawyer examines those decisions to understand whether they reflect isolated exceptions or a broader change in how customers buy the company’s services. The lawyer finds that prospective customers are increasingly requesting short, narrowly scoped pilots before committing to ongoing service agreements. The standard liability position was developed for those longer engagements. After assessing how the pilots’ limited data access and restricted use affect the company’s exposure, the lawyer concludes that these pilots warrant their own liability position. The existing position should continue to apply to ongoing service agreements. That decision requires more than knowing the standard terms. It requires understanding the reasoning behind them, identifying which facts change the answer, and knowing where the original position should still hold. The lawyer revises the Skill to explain the pilot position and its limits. The instructions specify what to check about duration, permitted use, and data access, along with the departures that still require escalation. blogs.content: Introducing Ontological Legal Research | Legora Product Solutions Security Customers Company Resources Log in Book a demo Menu Log in Product Updates Introducing Ontological Legal Research Introducing Ontological Legal Research Category Product Updates published Oct 29, 2026 author Team Legora Today, we’re introducing Ontological Legal Research, starting with the United States. It brings comprehensive legal data together with a proprietary ontology that maps how sources connect. This enables the Legora Agent to see the full picture of current law and navigate it with unprecedented accuracy. One of the hardest problems in legal AI AI fails at legal research in critical ways. Fabricated citations are the most visible failure. Even when the sources are real, AI can cite outdated law, misjudge a source’s authority, or find the main rule but miss the exception. It misses the full picture of current law. Fixing this takes two things: comprehensive legal data and a way for the Agent to understand how the law connects. Whatever it takes to get comprehensive data The single most common frustration we hear from customers is that you can't get the best data and the best technology in one product. Legal publishers have comprehensive data but a weaker AI layer. AI providers have advanced technology but not yet comprehensive data for legal research. Too often, the data our clients buy access to is simply not available in the AI platforms they want to use — one prominent publisher CEO recently noted that only 1% of their data was actually available in a partner's platform. So we’re bringing comprehensive legal data into Legora. Primary law is a public asset, but getting hold of it is surprisingly difficult. The challenges vary by jurisdiction and source type. In Germany, only about 3% of case law is digital. In the UK, legislation from official sources is often two to four weeks behind. In the US, the court reporters are printed by publishers who won’t sell a digital copy. We partner wherever it enables us to deliver the best possible user experience, but where a partnership won’t deliver the right quality or coverage, we go directly to the source and get it ourselves: manual requests, physical scanning. Whatever it takes. Example from Swedish Supreme Court, excluding IP and scanned live. US case law is one example. The courts are clear that judicial opinions are a public asset (we brought in outside counsel to confirm), but publishers won’t sell a digital feed of citable cases. So we collect slip opinions directly from court websites within 24-48 hours, then get the physical advance sheets and bound volumes within about a week of release. We take the spines off, remove publisher-added material such as headnotes and annotations, then scan them. To get to 99.997% accuracy, three separate people check every word on every page. Our Attorney Editors bring decades of experience at traditional publishers. They map source coverage in each jurisdiction by document type, including required historical coverage and update frequency. Customer requests drive priorities, and our customers' law librarians help audit the comprehensiveness and accuracy of our data. Building a map of current law With the data in place, the second challenge is understanding how the sources connect, and what is current law. US legal sources alone span tens of millions of documents, far more than any AI model can process at once. blogs.content: Insights Find Every Auto Renewal Clause in Your Portfolio Before its Notice Window Closes An auto renewal clause can set a notice deadline months early. Sort contracts by renewal mechanism, map 30 to 180-day windows, and give each one an owner. by Harvey Team • Nov 6, 2026 An auto renewal clause, also called an automatic renewal clause, extends a contract for another term unless a party gives notice by a set deadline. Tracking that deadline on one agreement is simple. A portfolio multiplies the deadlines, and Zylo's 2026 SaaS Management Index found that the average organization manages 211 SaaS renewals annually, before IT services and facilities agreements are counted. Take a hypothetical in-house team with about 400 supplier agreements across SaaS, IT services, and facilities. In this example, 260 of them renew automatically on January 1 unless someone gives notice. Their notice periods run 30, 60, 90, or 180 days, so the deadlines fall anywhere from July 4 to December 1. Reading 400 agreements for the same few renewal facts is the slow part, and AI can take it on. Harvey's review tables pull each agreement's renewal terms into columns linked to the source clause, so the team's time goes to checking those facts and deciding what to renew. We'll follow this team from sorting its contracts to getting each owner's decision in before the notice deadline. An Auto Renewal Clause Extends the Term Unless Someone Gives Notice in Time An automatic renewal clause sets four facts to capture: the renewal term, the notice period, who can give notice, and how notice must be delivered. Here's a sample clause from one of the team's agreements, a $240,000-a-year analytics subscription, written for this example: "This Agreement will renew automatically for successive twelve (12) month renewal terms. Either party may prevent renewal by giving the other written notice of non-renewal at least sixty (60) days before the end of the then-current term. All notices must be delivered to the addresses set out in Section 14.2." Read as data, it gives a 12-month renewal term, a 60-day notice period, a right either party holds, and a delivery rule that points to Section 14.2. A contract auto renewal clause often splits those facts across sections, so the notice address may sit in a general notices clause or in a later amendment. Missing any one of them can leave a notice of non-renewal open to challenge. The Renewal Mechanism Decides Whether Silence Keeps a Contract or Ends it Before any date matters, each contract needs a label for what happens if nobody acts. An auto renewal contract keeps running on silence, while an option to renew lapses on silence, so the two call for opposite actions. Here's how the team's 400 agreements sort, with all counts hypothetical: Renewal mechanism What happens if nobody acts Who has to act, and by when Agreements in this example Automatic renewal for a fixed term The contract renews for the stated renewal term The party that wants out, by giving notice of non-renewal before the notice deadline 300, including the 260 that renew on January 1 Evergreen, terminable on notice The contract keeps running, often month to month, until someone ends it The party that wants out, by giving notice that takes effect after the notice period 45 Option to renew The contract expires at the end of its term The party holding the option, by exercising it before its deadline 25 Fixed expiry The contract ends on its stated date Both parties, by signing a new agreement or an extension before that date 30 Some lawyers use "evergreen clause" for any automatic renewal, and others reserve it for contracts with no fixed renewal term, as the table does. Whichever label your team uses, record what silence does, since that decides whether a contract has a deadline to watch. The rest of this example follows the 260 January 1 renewals. blogs.content: Product Introducing Harvey’s Fact Graph for Disputes, Litigation, and Investigations The Harvey fact graph helps disputes, litigation, and investigations teams find and connect facts across millions of documents and build on one evolving record. by Harvey Team • Nov 5, 2026 We’re introducing Harvey’s fact graph, a new capability for disputes, litigation, and investigations teams to find and connect facts across millions of documents. It links those facts to supporting sources, to one another, and to the people, events, and issues they concern—helping teams uncover relationships across the full record over the lifetime of a matter. The fact graph is the newest addition to Harvey Graph , the connected map of legal knowledge and matter context that Harvey’s agents draw on to find the right information, cite it, and carry it forward. From Individual Facts to a Strategic Narrative In litigation and investigation matters, the job is to connect thousands of facts into a strategic narrative: who knew what and when, whether accounts hold up against the evidence, and where the record has gaps. The facts of a matter often seem disconnected, and the work requires ongoing resources to comb through huge volumes of information. An email might show that an executive received a warning about a defect. Meeting notes months later might record their approval of a product launch despite knowledge of the defect. Extracting and connecting those facts helps teams trace actions, assess what the evidence supports, and identify what still needs to be established. Harvey’s fact graph makes those connections across millions of documents, so teams can focus on judgment instead of piecing together the record. It extracts facts from each document, links back to the exact line of text, and connects events across the record, even when related facts seemingly appear disconnected or sit years apart. As new documents are added over time, the fact graph extracts new information, connects it to the existing record, and flags inconsistencies. New evidence or research can fill a gap, challenge an earlier account, or reveal the significance of a detail found months before. Each new document adds to what the team already knows, and the record grows with the matter. Turn Connected Facts Into Work Product Keeping the factual record current is just the foundation. Teams can also carry those facts into chronologies, witness outlines, memos, and reports. Instead of manually updating work product, Harvey keeps the context up-to-date and flags where prior work is outdated. With the fact graph, teams build work product on the same evolving record throughout the life of a matter. Agents in Harvey draw on the facts and connections already established to generate first drafts, from witness interview outlines early in an investigation, to deposition memos as evidence builds, to preparation materials for a hearing or trial. Each stage builds on the team’s accumulated understanding, so no one has to reconstruct the factual context for each new task. Build on Prior Work as Your Matter Progresses Matters can run for years, outlasting the teams that first worked on them. New team members join, responsibilities shift, and new counsel may come in just weeks before trial. Getting up to speed often means reviewing documents again, piecing together earlier analysis, and relying on handoff conversations to understand what the team knows and why. The fact graph keeps the matter’s facts, supporting sources, review decisions, and work product together, so understanding persists through every phase of the matter. Incoming teammates or counsel can easily trace the audit log, see how the team assessed earlier information, and identify inconsistencies. Every member of the team has a starting point that reflects months or years of accumulated work, so they spend less time reconstructing the matter and more time preparing for what comes next. blogs.content: Precedent New York 2026: The conversations defining the future of legal work | Legora Product Solutions Security Customers Company Resources Log in Book a demo Menu Log in Events Precedent New York 2026: The conversations defining the future of legal work Precedent New York 2026: The conversations defining the future of legal work Category Events published Oct 27, 2026 author Team Legora A little over three years ago, Legora didn’t exist. Last week, we welcomed 250 legal leaders to The Guggenheim in New York for Precedent, our flagship global summit. A lot has changed since the last Precedent at London’s Royal Opera House just six months ago. Legora now serves over 2,400 customers in over 80 markets. The energy in the room was something special. Frank Lloyd Wright’s Guggenheim was built by people who refused to accept that things had to look the way they always had. That’s a precedent worth keeping. It felt like the right room to gather the people who spend their days rethinking legal work. Many of them have shaped Legora along the way. “You push us, you challenge us, and you tell us when things need to get better,” said Legora CEO Max Junestrand, “and we do the same for you.” It was a special night. During the evening, we heard Ramp Co-Founder and Co-CEO Eric Glyman share his insights on finance’s AI transition, legal leaders from Salesforce, Venable, and Microsoft talk about what’s working and what’s next. Max Junestrand also took to the stage with a packed set of announcements, updates and the launch of Ontological Legal Research, which he called “the single biggest thing we have ever worked on.” Some key themes emerged from the fireside chats and panels: The industry has graduated from AI 101 Just a couple of years ago, discussions about AI’s impact on the future of legal work might have been theoretical, but as Legora CFO, David Eckstein, observed in his opening remarks, “we are way past that.” Panelists agreed. Salesforce’s Erica Swainson said her team has moved from prompting basics to model selection, and Venable’s Stuart Ingis said that “rather than our lawyers learning the tools, the tools have learned our lawyers.” Revenue upside, not just efficiency, is showing up in the data. Ramp sees AI-forward companies pulling ahead, and with about 1% of U.S. corporate payments flowing through it, it has a better view than most. Glyman said Ramp’s own growth has accelerated even as it scales, and Ingis reported Venable’s most profitable quarter ever. Laying the foundations before you can move fast Microsoft’s Thomas Daemen leads a 178-person legal team supporting a sales organization that must add roughly $50 billion in revenue a year. Adding headcount couldn’t be the answer, he told The L Suite’s Erika Fisher; technology had to be. It took a year just to get Microsoft’s data estate in order before AI could deliver real value. Once it was in place, the payoff was what Daemen called a “canonical win-win-win”: sellers benefit from a lower cost of sales, the legal team can close deals more efficiently, and customers get answers sooner and a smoother contracting process. It has also changed how legal is perceived. Ticketing data often shows that the clause under fire is an engineering or business-model issue, not a legal one, so legal is no longer seen as the “blocker.” Adoption is a people problem, and requires grace. In his chat with Max Junestrand, Glyman said AI isn’t just about adopting new tools but an entirely new way of working, and it requires some grace and space as we learn it. He modeled this by sharing his own first attempts with Claude Code in front of the whole company, and urged leaders to set up IT access and permissions early and to potentially tolerate a “bad month” of spending so teams reach their first “aha” moment sooner. blogs.content: Insights AI Fluency in Legal Hiring and How to Show it “Comfortable with AI tools” in a job description tells candidates very little. Instead, firms can offer a common scale for AI fluency that shows students and junior lawyers what firms expect, and gives them a way to prove themselves fluent. by Peter Duffy • Nov 5, 2026 AI fluency is fast becoming a hiring priority for law firms. It means knowing how to use AI effectively in legal work, recognize its limitations, and apply your own judgment to its outputs. For students thinking about recruitment, that raises a practical question: What exactly do firms want students to know regarding AI, and how do you show you’ve got it? A few firms are leading the way with clarity around expectations. One recruitment post I came across recently opened with a single question: “Are you a lawyer who builds?” The post didn't come from a legal tech start-up or an alternative legal service provider, but a newly launched AI-forward practice set up by a leading European law firm. To explain what it meant, the firm pointed candidates to Levels 4 and 5 of Harvey’s recently published AI Fluency Framework : Builders , who create reusable AI tools such as agents and playbooks, and Catalysts , who build for others and set the standards around them. From AI Familiarity to Clear Expectations A few years ago, it would have been unusual to see law firms recruit explicitly for Builders and Catalysts. In the case of the aforementioned recruitment post, the firm made it clear that it needs lawyers who create with AI, not just use it, and it used the framework's levels to outline their expectations. This example shows how the ideal candidate profile has changed and what law firms are looking for specifically — not just an introduction to AI but the ability to build agents and think critically about how and when to use AI, pointing to a clear framework to attain and measure those skills If firms and candidates share a common language for AI fluency, the framework works just as well at the hiring stage as it does for a junior lawyer in development inside the firm. A firm built around AI is likely to be a step ahead of the wider market, but its hiring expectations are an early sign of where recruiting is heading, and quickly. Among the most progressive firms, AI fluency is already a skill set in rising demand. Expectations are getting clearer — and higher. For students, that makes it worth understanding those expectations now, before they become the norm. The Problem With "Comfortable With AI Tools" Look beyond the most AI-forward employers, and the picture is less precise. Those gates still decide who approves the deal and who signs, but they say little about who should decide a term that moved away from your standard position. See a sample clause, consent and merger rules, and a review table. by Harvey Team • Nov 3, 2026 An assignment clause says whether a party can transfer its rights or obligations under a contract to someone else, and on what terms. A restrictive version, often called an anti-assignment clause, requires the other party's consent or limits transfers to named exceptions. A change of control clause can extend that restriction to a sale of the party itself. When a business reorganizes, sells a unit, or raises money, those clauses decide which contracts go with the business. Take a hypothetical software company, OpCo, that's moving its payroll analytics product line into a new wholly owned subsidiary, NewCo. The move covers 240 contracts, including customer agreements, supplier contracts, inbound software licenses, and an office lease in San Jose. About a year later, an outside investor plans to buy 30% of NewCo, and a lender plans to extend a credit line secured by NewCo's receivables. Every company, contract count, and clause in this example is hypothetical. OpCo will transfer the contracts directly, so the reorganization is an assignment of contract rights and duties from OpCo to NewCo. The 240 contracts mix services, sales of goods, software licenses, and a lease, and each type follows its own rules. Results turn on each clause's wording and governing law, so counsel confirms each conclusion for the states involved. Sorting 240 contracts by hand means reading the same few clause types again and again. AI changes that step. Harvey's review tables, for example, pull each contract's assignment terms into columns counsel can check against the source, so lawyer time goes to the consents and judgment calls. Either party may assign this Agreement to an Affiliate, or to a successor to the business it relates to, on written notice and without consent (4) . A Change of Control of a party is deemed an assignment (5) . Any attempted assignment in breach of this Section is void (6) ." Sixty percent of contracts had drafting errors. When a self-driving car crashes, it makes the news. The scrutiny is warranted, but the headlines obscure the baseline. Human drivers cause far more crashes . They happen every day, yet almost none become media stories. In legal work, AI hallucinations also get the headlines. An AI-generated legal brief citing non-existent case studies. A judge who used AI to create a restraining order and misquoted state law. These are real issues that deserve attention. But Spellbook sees a different side to AI’s impact on legal and contract workflow. We see the human mistakes that are made when volume and complexity are met with limited hours and manual review. In fact, our data shows saved hours, greater accuracy and increased output when AI is deployed. So we decided to dig into the data to prove what we already know intuitively—humans make mistakes too. Using Spellbook Reviews, we analyzed 3,000+ SEC-filed contracts from over 500 companies, spanning 22 years. These were executed agreements from some of the largest and most heavily lawyered companies in the world. The findings showed plenty of interesting trends and fun examples. Six in ten contracts contained drafting issues. Many were minor. But one in 40 was high-risk—defined as changing the meaning of an agreement in a substantially negative way for at least one party—and they were concentrated in provisions that decide who gets paid, who carries the liability, and what happens in a dispute. None of this is a matter of carelessness by lawyers so much as a consequence of the length, complexity, and disjointed nature of how these types of SEC-filed agreements are prepared and negotiated. In this context, mistakes are inevitable. But they don’t have to be. Every company, public or private, will eventually run its contracts through products like Spellbook that will not only spot errors and risks immediately but suggest fixes based on a company’s own agreement context and real-time market data. Issue Example: A loan cap written two different ways. A mining company's loan agreement set its borrowing limit at "One Million Five-Hundred Sixty Thousand Dollars," then printed the figure beside it as $1,750,000.00. The words and the number differ by $190,000, and the mismatch appears twice. If the borrower and lender ever disagree, the contract gives a court no clear answer, and $190,000 turns on who wins. Findings at a Glance This study should be treated as a proxy for how much humans miss. We kept our analysis deliberately narrow, counting only objective drafting mistakes we could verify from the document itself. We could not judge whether an agreement was signed out of policy, drifted off market, or if a company gave away more than it should, let alone what sits inside the millions of private contracts. These numbers should be thought of as the floor, not a full account of everything worth fixing in an agreement. blogs.content: Insights Turning a Raw Deposition Transcript Into a Usable Record Learn how litigation teams turn deposition transcripts into source-linked, usable records for case strategy, drafting, and trial preparation. by Harvey Team • Oct 29, 2026 By the time a deposition ends, a litigation team may have hundreds of pages of testimony and very little time to turn it into something useful. The transcript preserves what was said, but it doesn’t tell you which admissions matter, where a witness’s account shifted, which exhibits carry the point, or how the testimony fits with the rest of the record. An AI deposition summary can shorten that first pass. What’s more valuable is a working record organized around the issues in dispute, linked back to the underlying testimony, checked against the operative transcript, and structured for whatever the team needs to do next. A Deposition Transcript is the Record, but Not a Working Case Tool Depositions are organized in the order that questions were asked, not necessarily in the order a lawyer will later need the facts. Witnesses might discuss the same issue at several points, qualify an answer thirty pages later, or refer to an exhibit that only becomes important once another witness is deposed. A usable record reorganizes that testimony around the case. It should make it easy to see what the witness admitted or denied, where the account changed, what events belong on the chronology, which documents matter, and where the team needs to follow up. This way, the transcript remains the source of truth, while the working record makes it more efficient to use. Before Summarizing, Confirm Which Version of the Transcript You’re Working From Transcript analysis gets harder to trust when the team isn’t clear on which version sits underneath it. Before you summarize, extract, or compare testimony, identify whether you’re working from a rough transcript, a final transcript, or a version that’s been corrected. Distinguish a Rough Transcript From the Final Certified Record A rough transcript can be useful when the team needs to start analysis immediately after the deposition. Treat that work as provisional, though. Wording, formatting, and page-line references may change before the final certified transcript is available, so check quotations and pinpoint references again before using them in a filing, examination outline, or other work product. Incorporate Corrections and the Errata Sheet If the witness later makes permitted changes, those updates need to travel with the analysis. In federal practice, Rule 30(e) provides a process for reviewing the transcript or recording and listing changes and the reasons for them when review was requested before the deposition ended. Other jurisdictions may handle the process differently, but the practical point is the same. A summary created before an errata sheet or other correction is incorporated may no longer reflect the operative record. Preserve the Source Structure From the Beginning Keep the reference information that helps a lawyer get back to the testimony quickly. This typically includes page and line numbers, speaker, exhibit references, and any other useful transcript markers. Stripping those details out may make a summary look cleaner, but it also makes every important finding harder to verify and cite later. Choose the Deposition Summary Format Based on What the Team Needs to do Next No single deposition summary format works for every task. The right structure depends on the job the summary needs to support, and the same transcript may justify more than one output. Page-Line Summaries Make Precise Testimony Easier to Retrieve Use a page-line summary when the team expects to return to exact testimony often. These work especially well for impeachment preparation, motion drafting, witness outlines, and any task where the reader needs a concise description of the answer next to a clear and precise source reference. blogs.content: Insights Extending Legal Agent Bench to U.S. Case Law Introducing a new extension to Legal Agent Bench that tests frontier models’ ability to research and draft litigation briefs end-to-end using real case records. by Laura Toulme and Julio Pereyra • Oct 29, 2026 Today we introduce LAB: United States Case Law (LAB: USCL), an evaluation framework for testing frontier models’ ability to research and draft litigation briefs end-to-end using real case records. LAB: USCL adds novel approaches to LAB for understanding model behavior by building environments from real, public data collected by Free Law Project and evaluating model-written briefs head-to-head. We find that a small group of frontier models can now research and write complete, first-draft briefs in a single shot with no attorney guidance. While these briefs still exhibit a long tail of failure modes, they are substantially closer to the high bar for filing with a court and mark a substantial advance on a task that demands complex legal reasoning and advocacy. In this post we discuss our initial findings on these emerging capabilities as well as how we plan to make research in this area more accessible in partnership with Grubel. Brief Writing: An Ultra-Long Horizon Task When parties to a litigation want a court to act, they file a motion: a formal request asking the judge to issue a specific order or ruling. A motion may ask the court to do routine things like change a deadline or take more dramatic actions like dismissing a case or sanctioning a party. Some motions are opposed by the other parties, who argue that it would be legally incorrect or otherwise inappropriate for the court to take the requested action. To support these more contested motions, parties file briefs: written advocacy explaining why the court is justified in taking some action based on the state of the case, the law and precedent, and other considerations. Brief writing is one of the most complex tasks in litigation, sometimes requiring a team of lawyers multiple weeks to write and refine a compelling argument. An agent replicating this work must complete the same three steps a lawyer does: understanding the state of the case, researching the case law, and writing the brief itself. Understanding the State of the Case. For agents, the first part of replicating this work is understanding the state of the case by reviewing its docket, the official record of the case’s proceedings. The docket lists every filing, meaning every document submitted to the court, such as the complaint that starts the lawsuit, the motions and briefs that contain the parties’ arguments, and exhibits supporting those arguments, such as contracts, letters, or financial records. It also records the judge’s orders and rulings. In complex or long-running cases, the docket can span thousands of filings. Figure 1. A sample PACER docket with identifying details anonymized. A docket lists filings and court actions in chronological order, with hyperlinks to download the underlying documents. Researching Case Law. The next step is case law research: finding the past court decisions that bear on the legal questions in a case and determining how much weight each one carries. When judges rule on motions or decide cases, they often explain their reasoning in written opinions. Together, these opinions make up case law, the body of rules that comes from judges’ decisions, as opposed to rules passed by legislatures (statutes) or issued by agencies (regulations). These decisions carry weight because they create precedent. In the United States legal system, judges are expected to justify their decisions by relying on earlier opinions. Some of those opinions are binding: a court must follow decisions on the same legal question from higher courts in its jurisdiction. blogs.content: Insights ESI Protocol Best Practices for Search Terms and Production Format Before Discovery Starts Learn how to negotiate ESI protocol search terms, production formats, metadata, and change procedures before discovery begins. by Harvey Team • Oct 28, 2026 ESI protocol disputes rarely start with a disagreement about whether electronically stored information should be produced. Instead, the friction is typically over what gets searched, how the search is run, and whether the production arrives in a form counsel can actually use. These decisions are much easier to resolve before collection, review, and production are already in motion. In federal litigation, Rule 26(f) requires the parties’ discovery plan to address issues involving electronically stored information, including the form or forms of production. Rule 34 allows a requesting party to specify a production form and set defaults when no form has been agreed. An ESI protocol is one way to turn those obligations into practical rules for the matter, although the Federal Rules do not require every case to use a document with that title. However, timing matters — once a team has reviewed a large population under one search approach or begun producing data in an agreed format, changing course can create avoidable rework and new disputes. This guide focuses on two decisions worth settling early: search methodology and production format. For broader lifecycle context, see our eDiscovery guide for law firms . Key Takeaways: Negotiate the methodology, not just the keywords: A list of terms does not show how a search will be scoped, tested, or refined. Agreeing on the methodology upfront gives both sides a clearer basis for judging whether the search is reasonable and reduces the risk of expensive rework later. Test assumptions before they become protocol language: Hit counts alone cannot tell you whether a query is finding the right material or missing known responsive documents. Sampling and comparing results before the protocol is finalized can surface problems while the parties still have room to adjust. Choose production formats for how the evidence will be used: Native files, images, searchable text, and metadata preserve different kinds of context and functionality. Resolving those choices early makes the resulting production easier to review, analyze, cite, and defend. Build change into the protocol from the start: New custodians, data sources, terminology, or technical constraints often emerge after discovery begins. A defined process for revisiting search and production decisions keeps ordinary course corrections from turning into avoidable disputes. An ESI Protocol Should Resolve the Hard Choices Before the Data Starts Moving A useful ESI protocol reduces ambiguity before ambiguity becomes expensive. It should tell the parties enough about preservation, search, review mechanics, and production that each side understands the operating rules of discovery. It should also leave room for the facts to change. Keep in mind that this doesn’t mean that every case needs the same level of detail. A protocol for a focused contract dispute might look very different from one involving dozens of custodians, collaboration platforms, databases, and years of communications. The goal is not to reproduce a model order. It’s to identify the decisions that could materially affect scope, burden, usability, or later motion practice and resolve as many of them as practical at the outset. Courts may also expect counsel to address ESI early. For example, the Northern District of California’s ESI Guidelines and Checklist are meant to be consulted at the beginning of a case and specifically direct attention to preservation, search methodology, and production format. Local rules, standing orders, and judge-specific practices should therefore be part of the preparation, not an afterthought. blogs.content: Insights Drafting a First Answer to a Complaint From Exemplars Learn how litigation teams can draft an answer to a complaint from firm exemplars, current matter facts, and verified sources with AI-assisted workflows. by Harvey Team • Oct 28, 2026 When a complaint lands, the real work is turning a new set of allegations into a defensible response under deadline, while making sure facts, procedural choices, and client strategy belong to this matter (not the last one). Most firms already have useful prior work, so a relevant answer from a similar case can show how the team structures responses, handles recurring allegations, and frames defenses. At the same time, it can also create risk if old facts, outdated law, or case-specific strategy carry over unnoticed. A better workflow starts with the current complaint, confirms the procedural posture, finds the right exemplars, drafts against verified matter facts, and then compares the result back to both the complaint and the precedent set. In this article, we’ll look at how AI can speed up the document-heavy parts of that process, while ensuring that counsel still owns the choices that affect the client's position. Before Drafting, Confirm That an Answer is the Right Response Before starting a draft, confirm that an answer is actually the next filing that the matter requires. In federal court, Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12 governs the timing of responsive pleadings and allows certain defenses to be raised by motion. State rules, local rules, standing orders, and case-specific deadlines can change the analysis. That matters because some procedural choices have sequencing consequences. In federal practice, Rule 12(b) motions generally must be made before the responsive pleading when a responsive pleading is allowed, while Rule 12(c) provides for judgment on the pleadings after the pleadings close. Drafting first and analyzing posture later can narrow options the team meant to preserve. Before drafting, we recommend confirming: The court, jurisdiction, and governing rules. The service date and response deadline, which in federal court, is generally 21 days after service of the summons and complaint to answer. If the defendant timely waives service, that period can be extended to 60 days after the waiver request was sent, but a Rule 12 motion can change the timeline as well (typically due 14 days after notice that the motion was denied). Whether counsel is evaluating a pre-answer motion or another response. The claims, parties, requested relief, and any responsive claims that require analysis. Any local rules, standing orders, or judge-specific requirements affecting form or timing. Those answers also define what makes a prior answer relevant. For example, an exemplar from the same court and claim type may be far more useful than a more recent filing from a different procedural setting. What a First Answer to a Complaint Needs to Accomplish Once the response path is clear, an answer has three core jobs: Respond to the allegations. State the defenses and other responsive claims counsel intends to assert. Comply with the filing requirements that apply to the case. The document may look familiar, but each of those jobs depends on the current record. Respond to the Complaint's Allegations In federal court, Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 8 requires a responding party to admit or deny the opposing party’s allegations and permits a statement of insufficient knowledge or information to operate as a denial. If only part of an allegation is true, the rule calls for admitting that part and denying the rest. That makes complaint parsing more than an administrative step. Each numbered allegation needs a deliberate response tied to the facts the team can support. A fluent paragraph copied from an exemplar is less useful than a structured map showing what’s admitted, denied, partly admitted, or still needs factual investigation. Harvey’s Deputy General Counsel, Vineet Shahani, explains how a connected intake process can move legal work forward from the moment a request arrives. by Vineet Shahani • Oct 27, 2026 Requests to the legal team rarely arrive through one channel. A contract may come through email, a policy question through Slack, a marketing review through a design tool, and a product review may arrive by email with supporting documents in Google Drive. For the business, it can be difficult to know where to go for legal advice or who is the right lawyer for a particular request. Once a request reaches the legal team, they may need to follow up for missing context and find the relevant policies or precedents before review can begin. The team then identifies the right reviewer, reassigning the request if priorities or capacity change. Even for recurring requests, they may have to repeat these steps from scratch. A better intake model should move the request toward resolution from the moment it arrives. AI can support that process by helping gather the necessary context, applying the company’s legal standards, and directing each request to the appropriate member of the legal team, whether a contract manager, lawyer, or paralegal. Business teams get the guidance they need sooner, while lawyers spend less time coordinating and reviewing playbooks and precedents and more time applying their expertise. What Slows Legal Requests Down A request entering the legal team’s queue doesn’t necessarily mean it’s ready for review. A business stakeholder may know the outcome they need, but not the facts a lawyer needs to advise them. A customer’s marked-up MSA, for example, may arrive without the deal value, signing deadline, or context on what the parties have already discussed. The legal team then has to fill in the gaps by following up with the requester, locating the relevant documents and internal guidance, and determining who should handle the review. Even assigning the request can require coordination. The usual reviewer may be unavailable or at capacity, leaving someone to identify an alternative and transfer the context. By the time the request reaches the right person with the necessary information, days can pass. In the meantime, the business may move ahead or make commitments that leave the legal team with less room to advise. What appears to be a slow legal review is often just time spent preparing the request for legal review. This administrative burden becomes harder to sustain as demand for legal support grows without a corresponding increase in resources. In RSGI’s recent research , 68% of in-house legal teams expect their headcount to remain flat over the next year. Yet 92% of respondents reported faster turnaround of legal work to the business after adopting Harvey. That result points to how AI can help legal teams respond to business needs more quickly within existing capacity. Different Requests Need Different Paths Reducing time-consuming administrative work starts with recognizing that legal requests are not interchangeable. A marketing asset review may require details about the audience, claims, and supporting evidence before the legal team returns marked-up copy. A product review may involve a PRD, rollout plans, and input from several specialists before the business receives guidance on whether it can launch. Each request requires different context, expertise, and approvals. A fixed intake process struggles to account for those differences. If it asks too little, the legal team still has to gather the missing context. If it asks every possible question upfront, the process becomes burdensome and business users may avoid it. A team might review an offer letter in the morning, answer a handbook question before lunch, then open an employee complaint that later becomes an agency charge or litigation. The work changes, but the underlying burden is similar: find the right facts, compare them with company standards and applicable law, and turn that context into something counsel can review and act on. This is where legal AI is most useful because it can take a first pass on document-heavy work like drafting from approved precedent, structuring a complaint, building a chronology, comparing statements, or summarizing a demand letter. Lawyers still own credibility calls, risk tolerance, negotiation posture, and legal strategy. This article isn’t about automated systems used to screen candidates or make employment decisions. For in-house legal teams , the larger opportunity is primarily around connecting contracts, investigations, disputes, and institutional knowledge in one system instead of treating each task as a separate AI use case. Use AI to Draft and Review Employment Documents More Consistently Employment documents are repeatable, but they aren’t static. Offer letters, employment agreements, releases, handbooks, and disciplinary notices all need to reflect the organization’s current positions and the rules that apply in the relevant jurisdiction. Start First Drafts From Approved Templates and Precedent The best starting point is usually material your team already trusts. An AI draft based on an approved template, a prior agreement, and current instructions is more useful than one generated from a blank prompt because its starting point is already much closer to your organization’s actual standards. For example, counsel can use AI to prepare a first pass of an offer letter, employment agreement, separation agreement, NDA, or disciplinary notice, then review the terms that require judgment. Within Harvey, lawyers can also draft and edit in Word using precedents and source material from Vault or connected systems . For more information, our employment contract drafting guide dives deeper into the clause and jurisdiction decisions that employment teams need to make. Review Changes Against Your Standards For many teams, review matters more than generation. A counterparty redline, revised separation agreement, or updated form can be compared against approved positions to flag deviations, missing terms, and language that deserves a closer look. The lawyer then decides whether the change is acceptable, needs fallback language, or should be escalated. For repeatable review work, Contract Intelligence can review agreements against playbooks and precedent, surface deviations, and keep the review moving without turning approval into an automated decision. blogs.content: The CLOC Member Spotlight series profiles the incredible individuals within our community who are driving transformation in legal ops. Each spotlight provides inspiration, fosters connections, and gives readers a chance to learn more about their peers. By sharing these stories, we celebrate the diverse voices and talents that make CLOC a vibrant and connected community. November 2026 Member Spotlight: Frances Dupree Frances Dupree is the Strategic Customer Success Manager at Agiloft. She serves as the co-lead for CLOC Atlanta. Keep reading to learn more about Frances. About me : I’m a passionate Legal Operations professional, community leader, lifelong learner, and proud mother of nine. I currently serve as a Strategic Customer Success Manager at Agiloft, where I partner with organizations to drive meaningful outcomes through contract lifecycle management, strategic customer engagement, and technology adoption. My journey hasn’t followed a traditional path. As a former foster youth, I’ve learned the value of resilience, determination, faith, and creating opportunities even when the odds seem stacked against you. Those experiences have shaped my approach to leadership, my passion for helping others, and my belief that our beginnings do not determine our destinations. Throughout my career, I’ve worked across Legal Operations, legal technology, contract lifecycle management, eBilling, procurement, and operational transformation. I’ve had the privilege of helping organizations implement technology, improve processes, manage legal spend, and build more efficient and strategic legal functions. What excites me most is the opportunity to bridge the gap between people, processes, and technology while making a meaningful impact. I’m also honored to serve as a CLOC Atlanta Co-Regional Leader, helping cultivate a community where professionals can connect, learn, collaborate, and grow. Additionally, I’m the founder of OpsByFranny, LLC, where I channel my passion for education, knowledge sharing, and empowering others through Legal Operations insights and resources. Outside of work, I’m pursuing my MBA, raising my family, and embracing every opportunity to learn, lead, and serve. My faith and family are my foundation, and I believe deeply in the power of mentorship, authentic relationships, and opening doors for others. If there’s one thing I’d want my peers to know, it’s that I don’t measure success solely by professional accomplishments. I measure it by the relationships I’ve built, the challenges I’ve overcome, and the people I’ve been able to encourage along the way. I firmly believe that when one of us grows, we create opportunities for others to grow too. Why I love being a CLOC member : When I think about why I love being a CLOC member, one word immediately comes to mind: “community.” Not just professional networking or exchanging industry knowledge, but genuine relationships with people who see your potential, invest in your growth, and celebrate your success as if it were their own. My CLOC journey became especially meaningful because of one person: Delphina Turner. I met Delphina at an ACC conference, where we happened to sit next to each other at dinner. What seemed like an ordinary seating arrangement became one of the most meaningful connections of my professional journey. Delphina took me under her wing, and from that moment forward, she became so much more than a professional connection. She became my mentor, advocate, encourager, and someone who genuinely believed in me. She has encouraged me, advised me, challenged me, and, in the most loving way, pushed me beyond my comfort zone. There were moments when I questioned my own abilities, but Delphina saw something in me that I hadn’t fully recognized in myself. “She believed in me when I doubted myself.” That kind of mentorship is something you never forget,

blogs.author: AutoClaw
blogs.description: GLM-5.3 与 GLM-5.3-Flash 是分工不是替代：高频轻量任务用 Flash，复杂长程工程用旗舰，附任务分配标准与组合用法。
blogs.content: 返回博客 GLM-5.3 和 GLM-5.3-Flash 有什么区别？能力对比与场景选型 模型 作者：AutoClaw 2026年11月6日 GLM-5.3 与 GLM-5.3-Flash 是分工不是替代：高频轻量任务用 Flash，复杂长程工程用旗舰，附任务分配标准与组合用法。 GLM-5.3 和 GLM-5.3-Flash 有什么区别？能力对比与场景选型 同一个任务，用 GLM-5.3 跑还是用 GLM-5.3-Flash 跑，差别不在"谁更聪明"，而在"这个任务值不值得动用旗舰"。一句话给结论：高频、轻量、要快速反馈的日常工作，用 GLM-5.3-Flash；需要较少人工拆解、持续时间长、结果要求高的复杂任务，交给 GLM-5.3。两者是分工关系，不是替代关系——本文按官网公开口径把两者的能力、定位和适用场景讲清楚，帮你在 AutoClaw 里把任务分对模型。 先看速览：一屏分清两个模型 维度 GLM-5.3-Flash GLM-5.3 定位 GLM-5 系列首个原生多模态模型，面向高效编程与长程 Agent 任务 面向复杂工程与长程 Agent 任务的最新旗舰 架构特点 稀疏注意力与线性注意力混合架构，保持长上下文的同时显著降低计算开销 旗舰级 Agentic Coding，复杂工程与长程任务 在 AutoClaw 中的角色 高频、轻量、需要及时反馈的日常工作 需要较少人工拆解、持续时间更长、结果要求更高的任务 典型任务 截图理解、信息整理、文档处理、快速迭代 大型代码库、端到端开发、深度调试、长程研究 相对上一代 在多项基准与实际任务中超越 GLM-5.2 旗舰定位，承担最重的任务 维度一：定位不同，一个管快，一个管深 GLM-5.3-Flash 的关键词是"原生多模态 + 低开销"。它是 GLM-5 系列首个原生多模态模型，采用稀疏注意力与线性注意力混合架构，在保持精准长上下文能力的同时显著降低计算开销——翻译成使用体验：响应快、成本低、看得了图，适合一天要跑很多轮的工作。"原生多模态"意味着看图不是外挂能力：截图、图表、扫描件、设计稿这些视觉输入直接进模型理解，不用先转成文字描述再喂进去，中间环节的信息损失就此消失。 GLM-5.3 的关键词是"旗舰 + 长程"。它不只擅长生成代码，更能在大型项目中持续理解目标、处理多步骤依赖、使用工具并根据执行结果不断调整——从分析问题到执行、验证和交付，完整推进整个工作过程。这类任务的共同点是：中途不能断、步骤之间有依赖、错了要能自己排查着改。一个需求从设计、实现走到测试修复，中间任何一个环节断了都要重来的，就是它该接的活。混合架构对 Flash 的意义同样值得说透：长文档、长对话之所以在传统架构上又慢又贵，是因为注意力的计算量随长度暴涨；稀疏与线性注意力混合之后，长上下文仍然精准，但每个 token 的开销显著下降——这就是"又长又快"能同时成立的技术原因。 维度二：在 AutoClaw 里，它们分别接什么活 AutoClaw 支持模型切换（GLM 系列、DeepSeek 系列），两个模型的分工在官网模型页写得非常明确。GLM-5.3-Flash 适合处理图片、截图和视觉文档理解，图表、文件和信息的快速整理，文档、报告与内容处理，以及高频、多步骤的日常工作流——凡是需要快速反馈和持续迭代的任务，都是它的主场。 GLM-5.3 则面向复杂软件工程与大型代码库，从需求到实现的端到端开发，深度调试、代码重构与问题排查，多工具、多步骤工作流，以及长时间运行的研究和技术任务。它处理的是那些"中途不能断、错了要自己排查"的硬任务。 实际使用里还有第三种用法：同一任务的两个阶段用不同模型。比如一份长报告，先让 GLM-5.3 搭好结构和关键论证，再用 GLM-5.3-Flash 快速迭代格式、补图表、改措辞——重活在旗舰上做，轻改在 Flash 上跑，节奏和成本都更合理。 在 AutoClaw 里直接调用这两款模型 两个模型不需要分开安装、分开开通：它们都已内置在 AutoClaw 里，新建任务时直接选择即可，上下文、工作文件和交付物都在同一个工作区，切模型不打断工作。新模型上线即接入也是常态——GLM-5.3-Flash 发布当天就在 AutoClaw 可用，不存在等适配的窗口期。 具体到日常使用，常规任务默认直接下单，AutoClaw 会按任务特点匹配合适的模型；明确的复杂工程、长程研究、大型代码库任务，指定 GLM-5.3；高频轻量、多轮迭代的任务，指定 GLM-5.3-Flash。切换过程中已生成的工作文件和交付物不受影响——你可以在同一个项目里先用 GLM-5.3 打底，再切 GLM-5.3-Flash 做轻量迭代，反之亦然。项目做到一半换模型同样成立：文件、对话和已交付的产物都在，随时切。 任务光谱：常见工作的对号入座 把日常任务摊开，大部分都能在这张表里找到位置： 任务 推荐模型 理由 起草/修改邮件、文案、通知 GLM-5.3-Flash 单轮或少数几轮，快和迭代体验优先 截图、图表、扫描件转结构化数据 GLM-5.3-Flash 原生多模态主场 长文档摘要与要点整理 GLM-5.3-Flash 混合架构下长上下文开销低 多份表格合并、清洗、核对 GLM-5.3-Flash 规则明确的高频数据处理 月度/季度总结的素材聚合 GLM-5.3-Flash 量大、步骤多但单步轻 竞品研究报告（搜集到成稿） GLM-5.3 多工具搜集、交叉验证、长程成稿 端到端开发（需求→实现→测试） GLM-5.3 复杂工程与 Agentic Coding 深度调试与代码重构 GLM-5.3 大型代码库里的持续定位 长程研究任务（边查边验证） GLM-5.3 需要持续理解目标与多步骤依赖 一份长报告的框架与论证 GLM-5.3 结构与论证质量决定报告上限 同一份报告的第三轮修订 GLM-5.3-Flash 轻量迭代，反馈要快 定时批量任务（每日汇总、盯页面） GLM-5.3-Flash 高频连续执行，成本敏感 规律很清楚：看两件事——单次任务的工作量和整个流程的步数。工作量大、步骤之间有依赖的，往上选；量大但每步都轻的，往下选。 组合用法：一个项目里怎么让两个模型接力 真正提效的用法不是二选一，而是让两个模型在同一项目里接力。以一份竞品研究报告为例，官网公开能力支持这样的分工：GLM-5.3 负责需要持续理解目标的部分——拆解研究问题、多工具搜集与交叉验证、搭建报告骨架和关键论证；GLM-5.3-Flash 负责高频轻量环节——图表和资料的快速整理、逐轮的措辞修订、格式与排版迭代。重活在旗舰上做深，轻改在 Flash 上跑快，整份报告的节奏会比全程用一个模型更顺。 接力不需要复杂操作：在 AutoClaw 里按任务阶段切换模型即可，上下文和已交付的文件都在同一个工作区里。一个常见的节奏是把项目分成三段：开题和研究阶段用 GLM-5.3，把问题定义、资料基础和框架立住；制作阶段视内容重量灵活选择，重的论证继续用 GLM-5.3，轻的整理交给 GLM-5.3-Flash；修订和交付阶段几乎全程 GLM-5.3-Flash，因为这一阶段要的是快和多轮。 两种典型工作节奏，模型组合完全不同 看看两种真实的工作状态，模型搭配思路截然不同。一种是一天处理二十件小事的节奏：早上整理三份会议记录、上午归档一批截图资料、中午出两版文案、下午核对五张表——每件事都是单轮或少数几轮的轻任务，这种日子几乎全程 GLM-5.3-Flash，要的就是每件事都快、当天全清。另一种是一周跟一个长项目的节奏：周一立框架、周三中期检查、周五看阶段产出，任务始终悬着、依赖不断累积——这种日子 GLM-5.3 是主力，中途的边角活才切 Flash。 大多数人两种节奏都有。所以模型不是选一次定终身，而是跟着当天的工作构成走：小事扎堆的日子放开用 Flash，攻坚的日子把 5.3 派上去。 怎么发现你用错了模型 用错模型是有信号的。如果你发现自己在反复把背景贴回对话里，任务做着做着模型就忘了目标，需要你不断重申——这是长程任务用了轻量模型，该换 GLM-5.3。反过来，改几行文案也要等很久，是日常高频任务上了旗舰，换 GLM-5.3-Flash 立刻见效。多步骤任务中途丢依赖（第二步做完忘了第一步的约定），同样说明该用旗舰；而截图、图表这类视觉内容处理不动，则要想到 GLM-5.3-Flash 的原生多模态才是主场。长程任务跑着跑着质量下降，说明验证和收尾阶段应该留给 GLM-5.3 收官。 另外，AutoClaw 也支持切换 DeepSeek 系列模型；本文聚焦 GLM 两款模型的分工，系列内其它模型的定位见官网模型页。 GLM 家族的完整分工 把视野放大到整个 GLM 家族，官网模型页给出了清晰的分层：GLM-5.3 是复杂工程与长程任务的旗舰；GLM-5.3-Flash 用原生多模态和混合架构覆盖高频轻量场景；GLM-5.2 面向项目级上下文和长程交付，适合需要反复分析、修改和验证、要持续保持上下文的项目；GLM-5-Turbo 为连续运行的 Agent 工作流优化，接流程明确但步骤较多的标准化任务；GLM-5V-Turbo 主打视觉理解与视觉编程，看懂截图、界面和视频再转化为行动。五款模型在 AutoClaw 里都可切换，按任务特点各就各位即可。 常见误区 Flash 是"低配"，重要任务不敢用。 官网口径是它在多项基准与实际任务中超越 GLM-5.2——上一代旗舰级模型的能力水平，处理日常办公与轻量开发绰绰有余。选型看的是任务匹配，不是型号大小。

Copy page Copy page Releases v2.1.225 → v2.1.233 3 features · August 10–14 Auto-continue after a usage limit on Desktop Desktop When you hit your session limit in the Code tab of Claude Code Desktop, the limit card now offers an Auto-continue when limits reset checkbox. Check it, and the Desktop app retries the interrupted turn after the reset. The card shows the retry time. The weekly-limit card doesn’t offer it. The card shows Auto-resuming at followed by the reset time, and the turn picks up on its own once the limit resets. Subagents Claude spawns in interactive sessions, apart from the ones an agent-team teammate spawns, also run in the background by default. Start a fork yourself with a task that needs everything you’ve discussed so far: Claude Code > /subtask draft unit tests for the parser changes so far The fork appears in the panel below your prompt and its result arrives in your conversation when it finishes. To turn fork mode off, set CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT=0 . Turn fork mode on or off GitLab merge requests and marketplaces v2.1.232 Plugin marketplaces clone bare gitlab.com URLs, including nested subgroups. Copy page Copy page Releases v2.1.220 → v2.1.224 3 features · August 3–7 Cross-session messaging v2.1.224 Your Claude Code sessions can now message each other. Claude discovers your other sessions with the ListAgents tool and sends with SendMessage , either when you ask it to or on its own, such as after a change in one session affects what another is working on. A message is text Claude writes for the other session, never your conversation history or files. Available on macOS and Linux. Requires v2.1.224 or later. With two sessions open on the same machine, ask one of them to pass something along: Claude Code Tell the session working on the payments API that users.name is now users.display_name The other session shows a Message from row once Claude has read the message; press Ctrl+O to expand it. Run claude self-hosted-runner on your machines or containers to turn them into runners. When someone picks your environment while starting a session from claude.ai, the mobile or desktop apps, or claude --cloud , that session runs inside your network, with access to your internal services. An Owner turns on Allow self-hosted environments in admin settings first. Signed in as an Owner, run the guided setup, which walks you through creating the environment and starts a runner: terminal claude self-hosted-runner setup The environment shows Healthy in admin settings once the runner registers. blogs.content: What's New Week 30 · July 20–24, 2026 Copy page Copy page Opus 5 becomes the default Opus model, Claude Code Desktop adds an iOS Simulator pane, and the Claude Security plugin scans your code for vulnerabilities. Copy page Copy page Releases v2.1.214 → v2.1.219 3 features · July 20–24 Claude Opus 5 new model Claude Opus 5 is the new default Opus model in Claude Code. It’s the default on Max, Team Premium, Enterprise pay-as-you-go, and the Anthropic API, and on Claude Platform on AWS, Amazon Bedrock, and Google Cloud’s Agent Platform. On the Anthropic API and on Max, Team, and Enterprise plans, Opus 5 runs with a 1M-token context window ; on Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud’s Agent Platform, select the 1M model variant. Fast mode moves to Opus 5 at $10/$50 per MTok. Requires v2.1.219 or later. Switch to Opus 5 by name, or pick it from the model picker: Claude Code > /model claude-opus-5 Model configuration iOS Simulator in Claude Code Desktop Desktop Claude Code Desktop on macOS gets an iOS Simulator pane, in public beta on Pro, Max, and Team plans. When Claude builds, launches, or checks your app in a simulator, the pane opens next to the conversation and streams the device screen live, so you can watch Claude tap through the app to verify its changes or drive the device yourself. Requires Xcode with the iOS platform installed, and Claude Desktop v1.24012.0 or later. Ask Claude to run or test your app, and the pane opens when the app launches: Claude Code > Build the app and run it in the simulator to check the onboarding flow. blogs.author: AutoClaw Team
blogs.description: 三种桌面 AI Agent 路线六维度对比：安装、数据边界、执行、模型归属、成本、适合谁，附三个真实任务跑法与 30 秒决策表。
blogs.content: 返回博客 AutoClaw、Manus 和自部署开源 Agent 有什么区别？三种路线怎么选 产品 作者：AutoClaw Team 2026年11月6日 三种桌面 AI Agent 路线六维度对比：安装、数据边界、执行、模型归属、成本、适合谁，附三个真实任务跑法与 30 秒决策表。 AutoClaw、Manus 和自部署开源 Agent 有什么区别？三种路线怎么选 选桌面 AI Agent，本质上是在三种工作方式里选：装一个现成的（AutoClaw），在云端用（Manus），或者自己把开源的 Agent 框架跑起来（自部署）。没有哪条路线绝对更好，取决于你处理什么数据、做什么工作、愿意承担多少维护。本文把三条路线放进六个维度里对比，其中包括一个常被忽略的维度：底下的模型是谁做的。后文有 30 秒决策表。 我们怎么比的 下文每个维度都用同样的三个输入：各产品官方文档（截至 2026 年 11 月）、AutoClaw 自家工作流的使用经验，以及另外两条路线的公开资料。价格、集成、模型可用性这类经常变化的内容，请以各产品官网当前说明为准。 三条路线 AutoClaw（一键本地安装）。 智谱出品的桌面 AI Agent，一键安装在 Windows、macOS 上，直接操作你电脑里的文件、浏览器和工具。文件和操作留在本机，只有完成任务所需的内容会发送给模型。50+ 内置技能开箱即用；目标模式（设定目标，规划-执行-验证-迭代）、Agent 集群模式（并行多角色执行加复核）、定时任务、多 Agent 记忆隔离都有；飞书、企业微信、微信等 IM 可以直接接入使用。 Manus（云端原生）。 商业云端 Agent 平台。任务在 Manus 的云端环境执行：你在网页或应用里给出目标，它在云端分解、执行并交付。优势是无需安装、多设备体验一致、集成生态丰富（浏览器扩展、移动端等）。对应的取舍是任务跑在云端，文件需要上传，按套餐和用量付费。 自部署开源方案（以 OpenClaw 框架为代表）。 开源 Agent 框架社区活跃，自部署意味着最大的控制力和可定制性，也意味着最大的责任：环境搭建、API 密钥管理、安全加固、版本维护都由你负责。 选型前，先问自己六个问题 这六个问题的答案，基本决定了你该走哪条路线： 你处理的文件里有没有合同、财务、客户资料这类敏感内容？ 你的任务是每次都不一样，还是长期重复？ 团队里有没有人能管部署和运维？ 协作主要发生在哪个平台：飞书、企业微信还是浏览器？ 预算是固定订阅更好预测，还是可以接受随用量浮动？ 未来半年任务量是稳定、增长还是不确定？ 带着这六个答案往下读，每个维度的结论会自然对号入座。 维度一：安装与上手 AutoClaw Manus 自部署开源 安装 原生安装包，约 1 分钟 无需安装，浏览器/应用即用 数小时到数天（环境+配置+调试） 技术门槛 无 无 高（命令行、API、运维） 持续维护 官方自动更新 平台托管 版本与安全补丁自己负责 结论： 只想尽快开始干活，AutoClaw 和 Manus 都合适；自部署第一天的成本就高出一个量级。三种路线的"开始"成本结构不同：本地安装是装完即用，云端是打开即用，自部署是装完还要调。 维度二：数据边界 AutoClaw Manus 自部署开源 文件存储 文件留在本机，仅将任务所需内容发送给模型 上传到云端执行 自己掌控（取决于你的配置） 安全责任 官方更新维护，数据主要在本机处理 在平台方 完全在你 适合的数据 本地文件、日常办公与专业材料 一般办公材料 有安全团队的企业 三条路线最深的分界线在这里：文件放在哪里处理，谁来为它负责。AutoClaw 的文件和操作在你自己的电脑上，只有完成任务所需的内容会发送给模型；云端平台的文件需要上传到平台；自部署则完全取决于你自己的配置和纪律。 如果你每天处理合同、财务数据或客户文件，建议先看这一维度。需要注意：无论哪种路线，只要用到云端模型，相关内容就会发送给模型服务方。涉及保密协议的材料，请先确认协议是否允许使用 AI 服务，再决定怎么用。 维度三：执行位置决定能做什么 AutoClaw Manus 自部署开源 执行位置 本地，直接操作你的文件和浏览器 云端环境 你的基础设施 深度任务 目标模式自主循环 + 集群模式多角色复核 自主执行，模板生态丰富 取决于你的框架配置 IM 集成 飞书、企业微信、微信 以官方文档为准 自己搭 模型 默认 GLM 系列，可切换 DeepSeek 等 平台的模型矩阵 任意模型（自管 API） Agent 在哪里运行，决定了它能直接碰到什么。整理本地文件、操作你已登录的后台、批量处理磁盘里几十份扫描件、把一个本地大文件夹按规则归档重建，这些任务的原料和操作对象都在本机，本地 Agent 可以直接开干；如果用云端方案，通常要先解决文件怎么上传、登录态怎么提供的问题，具体做法以对应产品的官方文档为准。纯线上的资料搜集，云端和本地体验相差不大。 执行位置还影响持续跟进的形态。本地 Agent 可以通过定时任务每天在你自己的环境里跑检查，结果直接回到飞书、企业微信的会话里；云端方案的定时能力请参考各平台说明；自部署则要自己搭调度。 维度四：底下的模型是谁做的 这个问题常被忽略，但它会影响 Agent 和模型配合得有多紧。 AutoClaw 出自智谱，也就是 GLM 系列模型的同一家公司。新 GLM 发布后可以很快在 AutoClaw 里用到（GLM-5.3-Flash 就是这样），Agent 层也围绕 GLM 处理工具调用、长上下文和多步骤任务的方式做了适配。模型与 Agent 出自同一家公司，沟通链路更短。AutoClaw 同时支持切换到 DeepSeek 等其他模型，你可以按任务选择。 专业场景下，模型对专业材料的理解很关键。以法律工作流为例，AutoClaw 法律助手结合 GLM 模型与专业法律数据库检索，关键结论附来源，便于溯源复核。法律、金融这类领域，不同方案之间的差异往往更明显，建议用你自己的真实材料试一试。 Manus 使用平台选定的模型矩阵，自部署方案则由你自己提供 API 密钥。租用模型有灵活性，模型矩阵也有它自己的取舍。区别在于出了问题时找谁：用第三方模型，需要和模型供应商协调；AutoClaw 的默认模型和 Agent 出自同一团队。 这个维度什么时候重要？如果你的任务是通用型的总结和轻量自动化，模型归属影响不大；如果你在法律、金融、工程领域工作，值得放进决策表。 维度五：成本结构 AutoClaw Manus 自部署开源 前期 免费额度（核心功能+每日积分） 免费额度 硬件 + 你的时间 持续 订阅（个人/团队） 订阅 + 用量计费 API 成本 + 运维人力 隐藏成本 低 用量增长时需关注账单，先估算月度任务量 兼职运维的人力成本 自部署不一定贵在 API 费，维护时间长期容易被低估：安全补丁、版本升级、故障排查，每一项都是持续投入。按用量计费的服务，任务量上去之后账单也会跟着上去。订阅制最容易预测，花多少在签约时就定了。三种定价模式都合理，区别只在计费逻辑是否匹配你的用量曲线。具体价格与额度请以各产品官网为准。 算一笔具体的账：一个每天要跑十几次数据整理和文档处理的小团队，用订阅制，月费固定；用按用量计费的方案，需要按月盯着用量；用自部署，API 费用可能更低，但要摊进去一个懂运维的人力，这笔账在团队小的时候往往比订阅更贵。用量稳定适合订阅，波动大适合按量，有专职运维再考虑自部署。 维度六：各自适合谁 律师、法务、财务这类每天处理敏感文件的角色，AutoClaw 更适合：文件留在本机，法律工作流开箱即用，在飞书、企业微信、微信里直接可用。跨地区、协作密集的团队，做多语言协作、模板化任务、偏轻量的工作，Manus 的免安装和成熟集成更方便。工程团队和喜欢折腾的技术人，自部署开源方案给出最大控制，前提是你接得住对应的运维责任。 三者并不互斥。不少团队混用：敏感任务本地跑，开放调研云端跑，定制管道自部署。选型不是站队，是给不同类型的任务匹配合适的通道。 三个真实任务：同一件事，三种跑法 表格会藏住一些关键差异，所以拿三个日常任务，看三条路线分别怎么干。 场景 A："盯着订单看板，有异常就提醒我" 你开了家小店，想让 Agent 每 15 分钟检查一次订单看板，有异常就通知你。用 AutoClaw，你在飞书或企业微信里把目标说一次：定时任务在本机用你已有的登录态执行检查，提醒回到同一个会话，还附带看板截图，让你看到它看到了什么。用云端方案，要看看板是否公开可访问，以及登录态如何提供，具体做法以对应产品的官方文档为准。自部署也完全可行：自己写监控脚本、接提醒、管定时任务，灵活度最大，但你同时成了自己自动化的值班工程师。 场景 B："明天要签这份 40 页的合同，先帮我标出风险" 对方发来一份服务协议，你想在明天的电话前把风险标出来。AutoClaw 的法律助手模式下，文件放在你自己的电脑上处理，分析时只把任务所需内容发送给模型；它可以从你这一方的立场出发复核，输出 Word 修订稿，每条风险对应到具体条款。使用前请先确认合同的保密条款是否允许使用 AI 服务；AI 的结果建议由专业人员复核后再用于决策。用云端方案，则需要把文件上传到平台，是否可以，取决于你所在团队对文件外传的要求。自部署也能做，前提是你已经建好或接入了文档处理管道，并且信任自己加固的技术栈来处理法律敏感文件。 场景 C："每月出一份行业动态监测报告" 市场团队需要每月汇总行业新闻、竞品动向和公开数据，形成一份结构化的监测报告。AutoC

blogs.content: What's New Week 25 · June 15–19, 2026 Copy page Copy page Publish a live, shareable page from your session with Artifacts, match tool parameters in deny and ask rules, and set any setting from the prompt with /config. Copy page Copy page Releases v2.1.178 → v2.1.183 3 features · June 15–19 Artifacts An artifact is a live, interactive page that Claude Code publishes from your session to a private URL on claude.ai, and it updates in place as the session keeps working. Ask for one when terminal text is the wrong medium, such as a PR walkthrough with the diff annotated inline or a dashboard built from session data. Artifacts are in beta on Team and Enterprise plans. Ask Claude for a page, then approve the publish prompt: Claude Code Make an artifact that walks through this PR with the diff annotated inline. Create an artifact Match by input parameter v2.1.178 Deny and ask permission rules can now match a tool’s input parameters with the Tool(param:value) syntax. For example, Agent(model:opus) matches subagent spawns that request the Opus model tier. The value accepts * as a wildcard, so Agent(isolation:*) matches any explicit isolation value. Add a parameter rule to the deny list in settings.json : .claude/settings.json { "permissions" : { "deny" : [ "Agent(model:opus)" ] } } Match by input parameter Set any setting from the prompt v2.1.181 Pass key=value to /config to change a setting directly without opening the Settings interface. blogs.content: What's New Week 24 · June 8–12, 2026 Copy page Copy page Move a session to a new directory with /cd, let subagents spawn their own subagents, and troubleshoot a broken configuration with safe mode. Copy page Copy page Releases v2.1.166 → v2.1.176 3 features · June 8–12 Move a session with /cd v2.1.169 The new /cd command moves the current session to a different working directory without rebuilding the prompt cache: the new directory’s CLAUDE.md is appended as a message instead of replacing the system prompt. The session relocates to the new directory’s project storage, so --resume and --continue find it there. Claude prompts you to trust the directory if you haven’t worked in it before. Move the session into another project without restarting: Claude Code > /cd ../other-project Commands reference Subagents can spawn subagents v2.1.172 Subagents can now spawn their own subagents. The subagent panel below the prompt shows the full tree: each row carries a count of its descendants and a path back to main . Subagent chains are capped at five levels deep to prevent runaway concurrent trees. Open the agents view to watch the nested tree as work fans out: Claude Code > /agents Spawn nested subagents Troubleshoot with safe mode v2.1.169 Start Claude Code with --safe-mode , or set CLAUDE_CODE_SAFE_MODE , to launch with all customizations disabled: CLAUDE.md , skills, plugins, hooks, MCP servers, and custom commands and agents do not load. Authentication, model selection, built-in tools, and permissions still work. If a problem disappears in safe mode, one of those surfaces is the cause. Copy page Copy page Releases v2.1.139 → v2.1.142 3 features · May 11–15 Agent view research preview claude agents opens one screen for every Claude Code session: what’s running, what’s blocked on your input, and what’s done. Dispatch a bug fix, a pull request review, and a flaky-test investigation as three rows, keep working in another window, and step in only when a row needs you. Attach to any row to drop into its full conversation, then press ← to return to the list. Each background session keeps running without a terminal attached. Open the dashboard from your shell: terminal claude agents Agent view /goal v2.1.139 Set a completion condition and Claude keeps working toward it across turns without you prompting each step. After every turn, a fast model checks whether the condition holds; if not, Claude starts another turn instead of handing control back. Useful for substantial work with a verifiable end state, like migrating a module until every call site compiles and tests pass. The goal clears once the condition is met, and works in interactive, -p , and Remote Control. Set a goal and let Claude run until it holds: Claude Code > /goal all tests in test/auth pass and the lint step is clean Goals Fast mode on Opus 4.7 research preview /fast now runs on Opus 4.7 by default instead of Opus 4.6. Fast mode is a high-speed Opus configuration: the same model quality at about 2.5x the speed for a higher per-token cost, useful for rapid iteration and live debugging. Ask Claude to watch something while you keep working: Claude Code Tail server.log in the background and tell me the moment a 5xx shows up This pairs with /loop , which now self-paces: omit the interval and Claude schedules the next tick based on the task, or reaches for the Monitor tool to skip polling altogether. Copy page Copy page Releases v2.1.83 → v2.1.85 6 features · March 23–27 Auto mode research preview Auto mode hands your permission prompts to a classifier. Safe edits and commands run without interrupting you; anything destructive or suspicious gets blocked and surfaced. It’s the middle ground between approving every file write and running with --dangerously-skip-permissions . Cycle to auto with Shift+Tab, or set it as your default: ~/.claude/settings.json { "permissions" : { "defaultMode" : "auto" } } Permission modes guide Computer use Desktop Claude can now control your actual desktop from the Claude Code Desktop app: open native apps, click through the iOS simulator, drive hardware control panels, and verify changes on screen. It’s off by default and asks before each action. Best for the things nothing else can reach: apps without an API, proprietary tools, anything that only exists as a GUI. Enable it in Settings, grant the OS permissions, then ask Claude to verify a change end to end: Claude Code Open the iOS simulator, tap through the onboarding flow, and screenshot each step Computer use guide PR auto-fix Web Flip a switch when you open a PR and walk away. Claude watches CI, fixes the failures, handles the nits, and pushes until it’s green. No more babysitting a PR through six rounds of lint errors. After creating a PR on Claude Code web, toggle Auto fix in the CI panel. Auto-fix pull requests Transcript search v2.1.83 Press / in transcript mode to search your conversation. n and N step through matches. Finally a way to find that one Bash command Claude ran 400 messages ago. Open transcript mode and search: Claude Code Ctrl+O # open transcript /migrate # search for "migrate" n # next match N # previous match Fullscreen guide PowerShell tool preview v2.1.84 Windows gets a native PowerShell tool alongside Bash. Claude can run cmdlets, pipe objects, and work with Windows-native paths without translating everything through Git Bash. Opt in from settings: .claude/settings.json { "env" : { "CLAUDE_CODE_USE_POWERSHELL_TOOL" : "1" } } PowerShell tool docs Conditional hooks v2.1.85 Hooks can now declare an if field using permission rule syntax. Your pre-commit check only spawns for Bash(git commit *) instead of every bash call, cutting the process overhead on busy sessions. Scope a hook to git commits only: .claude/settings.json { "hooks" : { "PreToolUse" : [{ "hooks" : [{ "if" : "Bash(git commit *)" , "type" : "command" , "command" : ".claude/hooks/lint-staged.sh" }] }] } } Hooks reference Other wins Plugin userConfig now public: prompt for settings at enable time, keychain-backed secrets Pasted images insert [Image #N] chips you can reference positionally managed-settings.d/ drop-in directory for layered policy fragments CwdChanged and FileChanged hook events for direnv-style setups Agents can declare initialPrompt in frontmatter to auto-submit a first turn Ctrl+X Ctrl+E opens your external editor, matching readline Interrupting before any response restores your input automatically /status now works while Claude is responding Deep links open in your preferred terminal, not first-detected Idle-return nudge to /clear after 75+ minutes away VS Code: rate limit banner, Esc-twice rewind picker Full changelog for v2.1.83–v2.1.85 → Was this page helpful?
